table.title: EN · REST endpoints
table.md:
| Endpoint | Method | Auth | Rate limit | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/api/v1/users/{id}` | GET | Bearer | 600/min | Returns the public profile of a user, including display name, avatar URL and account creation date. |
| `/api/v1/users` | POST | Admin | 60/min | Creates a new user. Email addresses must be verified before the account becomes active. |
| `/api/v1/sessions` | DELETE | Bearer | 120/min | Revokes the current session token. |
| `/api/v1/exports/{jobId}/download` | GET | Bearer | 10/min | Streams a finished export as a gzip-compressed CSV file; returns 409 if the job is still running. |

understanding.purpose: A compact REST API reference table: readers find an endpoint, then check its method, auth requirement, rate limit, and description.
understanding.reading: Rows are read endpoint-first; the path is the row key, Method/Auth/Rate limit are quick qualifiers scanned across rows, and Description is read last as prose.
groups: Method, Auth, Rate limit: compact request constraints that belong together and are compared across rows
Endpoint: standalone row identifier and primary scan target
Description: free prose, secondary to route identification
keep_intact: full endpoint path and path parameters such as {jobId}
may_wrap: header labels such as Rate limit and Description
endpoint path only as a deliberate last resort when avoiding horizontal scroll

preferred.name: r2A
preferred.note: Keeps Endpoint intact (282), the constraint trio at their natural minima (76/67/89), and gives Description the smallest width that still yields 2 lines (370 = 349px text ≈ 2×335). Total 884px instead of 736–666, i.e. more scroll, but row heights drop from 106/153px to roughly 60px and the table becomes ~330px tall — the white space under the endpoint disappears, and Description becomes scannable prose instead of a 3-word ribbon. This is the best height-per-pixel-of-scroll trade in the set.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Refines r2A: keep Endpoint at 282px so no path splits, keep Method/Auth/Rate at their minimum intact widths, and reduce Description from 370px to 300px. This cuts overflow from 525px to 455px while still allowing long prose about three lines. It is the conservative choice when endpoint integrity matters most, though Auth and Rate remain off-screen at 360px.

acceptable.name: r1A
acceptable.note: Refines r0A. Keep Endpoint at 282 (full paths intact) and Rate limit at 89 (one-line header), but widen Description from 180 to 221, giving 200px of text. Typical descriptions then settle at about 4 lines instead of 5, reducing row heights from 129 to roughly 105 and total height from 485 to about 411. This accepts 40px more horizontal scroll (735 vs 695), but since the reader must scroll anyway, the width is spent on prose legibility and shorter rows.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: A deliberate lean toward less scrolling: Description at 244px (223px text) gives 3 lines, so rows are ~80px and the table ~410px tall, at a total of 758px — only 22px wider than r1A but with two fewer description lines per row. Use this if the reader's workflow is 'scroll rarely, read the description fully once'.

bad.name: r1B
bad.note: Fixes r0B's fatal endpoint split by restoring Endpoint to 282, and keeps the one-line Rate limit header at 89. Description drops from 180 to 151 (130px text), so the table narrows from 695 to 665 and overflow falls from 335 to 305. The cost is choppier prose at about 6 lines and taller rows (~584px total), but the row key stays intact and no words split. At the right-edge scroll position, Description, Rate limit, Auth, and part of Method remain together, preserving row context.
bad.why: Description is squeezed to 151px, producing 6-line cells and 153px rows; the table is still 666px wide, so it buys little horizontal relief at the cost of a 578px-tall, slow-scanning grid with large empty areas under Endpoint/Method/Auth.

bad.name: r2C
bad.note: The unexplored alternative: give Description its full one-line width (691) so every row is a single 36px line and the whole table is ~250px tall — a true spreadsheet-like reference. Total 1205px means heavy horizontal scrolling, but row rhythm is perfect, comparison across rows is trivial, and no cell is ever a ragged column of short lines. Worth it if the table is used for scanning/verifying rather than reading prose in place.
bad.why: Description is 691px wide (670px content), wider than the 360px viewport; after scrolling to Description the reader must scroll again within each line. The table is 1206px wide, over three viewports, for only one-line rows.

bad.name: r3B
bad.note: Compromise between intact and phone-first: Endpoint 216px wraps the longest path to about two lines while Endpoint+Method+Auth fill the first 359px; Rate limit and Description scroll. Description 300px keeps prose to about three lines. Total 748px, overflow 389px. This makes Auth visible without forcing the endpoint into three lines.
bad.why: Endpoint is reduced to 216px, splitting the longest path mid-word; code identifiers must stay intact. The 136px width saving still leaves a 749px table that overflows by 389px.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: New mobile-first idea: narrow Endpoint to 138px so Endpoint+Method+Auth+Rate fit exactly in 359px (138+76+67+78=359). Rate header wraps but its values stay intact. Endpoint paths wrap at slashes as the deliberate last resort. Description at 300px keeps prose to about three lines. Total 659px, overflow 300px, with all compact qualifiers visible in the first viewport.
bad.why: Endpoint at 138px causes four mid-word splits, and the Rate limit header wraps; paths become hard to copy and scan, and the table still overflows by 300px.

rationale: The endpoint is the table's key and its longest path needs 282px, so it must not be split; Method, Auth and Rate limit are short categorical columns and should stay one-line. Description is the only flexible prose column: r2A gives it 349px of content, enough for a comfortable mobile measure and at most three lines, while keeping rows compact. The table still overflows horizontally because the first four columns alone are 514px, but r2A lets each description line be read within one 360px viewport after scrolling to it. Narrower designs add tall rows; wider designs force line-level horizontal scrolling.

general: Size identifier columns to the longest unbreakable token; never split URLs, paths, IDs or code tokens to save width.
Keep short categorical columns such as method, status, auth and rate on one line; their width is cheap and wrapping them hurts scanning.
For a prose column on a narrow screen, target a measure that fits the viewport once the reader has scrolled to that column, not the whole table width.
When a table cannot fit, compare total width against row height: over-wrapping prose creates tall rows with large empty areas in the left columns.
specific: This table cannot fit 360px: Endpoint + Method + Auth + Rate limit already require 514px, so horizontal scrolling is unavoidable.
Endpoint must be at least 282px to keep /api/v1/exports/{jobId}/download intact.
Description one-line needs 691px, which is too wide for mobile; about 370px gives 349px content and a 3-line maximum.
Method/Auth/Rate limit minima are 76/67/89px; extra width there buys no legibility.

tradeoffs: r3A is 70px narrower than r2A but adds 47px of height and two more 3-line rows; a designer prioritizing minimum total width could choose it. r1A/r2B are narrower still but accept 4-line description cells. r2C optimizes for one-line rows and desktop scanning at the cost of a 1206px table and description lines wider than the phone viewport.
uncertain: Exact wrap thresholds are approximate, and the row-height data show some variation that may depend on font metrics. If the publication target were desktop rather than phone, r2C or a wider description could be defensible; if horizontal scrolling were forbidden, no no-split design is viable.

critique.good: Keeps the full endpoint path intact, preserves every method/auth/rate token, has no mid-word splits, and uses a one-line Rate limit header. Rows read as units and the 5-line descriptions are legible.
critique.problems: The table is 695px wide, overflowing the 360px box by 335px. At the phone viewport the first view shows only Endpoint and Method; Auth, Rate limit, and Description all require horizontal scrolling. Description still needs 5 lines, so the design pays a large horizontal cost without gaining compact rows.
critique.cause: Endpoint 282 + Method 76 + Auth 67 + Rate limit 89 = 514px before Description even starts. The 282px endpoint is irreducible, so overflow is structural. Description at 180px leaves only 159px for prose, which forces 5 lines.

critique.good: Narrower at 552px, so less horizontal overflow than r0A. Method, Auth, and Rate limit remain intact, and the table is visually compact horizontally.
critique.problems: The endpoint path breaks mid-word: '/api/v1/exports/{jobId}/download' becomes '{job' / 'Id}/download'. That destroys the row key. Description at 140px produces 7 lines and 176px rows, while Method/Auth/Rate limit cells sit in large empty vertical space. Rate limit's header also wraps.
critique.cause: Endpoint 190px is 71px below the 261px unbreakable path width, so the browser splits inside '{jobId}'. Description 140px leaves only 119px for text, producing 7 lines. The narrow endpoint and description create tall rows without solving the width problem.

critique.good: It fits entirely inside the 360px box with no horizontal scrolling. The first four columns are visible together, and the row order remains readable in principle.
critique.problems: The table is 2577px tall and nearly unreadable. Description becomes a 48px ribbon with about 5 characters per line; its header splits into 'De/scr/ipt/ion'. There are 61 mid-word splits, including endpoint fragments and prose words. Rows are 664–757px tall.
critique.cause: Endpoint 90px and Description 48px are far below their minimum unbreakable widths. The true no-split minimum is 282+76+67+78+106 = 609px, so 360px cannot hold this table without splitting words. r0C chooses splits everywhere to satisfy the box.

critique.good: Endpoint and Method both survive intact and on one line, headers never wrap, no mid-word splits, and Method/Auth/Rate limit sit shoulder-to-shoulder as a compact constraint block right after the row key. The endpoint path, which is the row's identity, is never mangled.
critique.problems: The box shows only Endpoint and Method (plus a clipped sliver of Auth); Rate limit and Description — the two columns a reader most needs after the route — are entirely off-screen. Worse, every row is 106px tall while the Endpoint cell holds a single 20px line: ~70px of dead white space under each path, repeated 4 times. The table reads as an empty grid with text pushed to the left edge.
critique.cause: Description got 221px (200px of text) so its prose wraps to 4 lines; those 4 lines set the row height for the whole row. Meanwhile the four left columns consume 282+76+67+89 = 514px before Description begins, so the table is 736px wide yet still starves the only column that needs width.

critique.good: Same strengths as r1A — intact endpoint, unwrapped headers, no word splits — and it is 70px narrower, so slightly less horizontal scroll.
critique.problems: Everything r1A does wrong, worse. Description at 151px becomes a 6-line ribbon of 3–4 words per line; rows balloon to 153px and the table to 578px tall. The endpoint column now has ~130px of blank space per row, so the visual weight of the table is white space rather than data. The reader scrolls right to find a description that is unreadable in a 130px measure anyway.
critique.cause: Trading 70px of table width away from Description cost 2 extra lines per row × 5 rows ≈ +160px of height. Description is the wrong column to squeeze: it is the only one with 670px of one-line content, so it is the only one whose width change moves row height at all.

critique.good: Keeps every endpoint path and all compact qualifiers intact. Description at 370px keeps long prose to roughly 2-3 lines, so the table is not excessively tall.
critique.problems: Still overflows by 525px. At 360px the reader sees only Endpoint and Method; Auth and Rate limit are off-screen, so the qualifier group cannot be compared. Row heights swing 36/83/60/36/60 because Description lengths wrap unevenly, so rows do not read as equal units.
critique.cause: Endpoint 282 + Method 76 + Auth 67 + Rate 89 already consume 514px, and Description 370 pushes the total to 885px. Description 370px gives 349px of text, wide enough for short prose to stay on one line but forcing long prose to three, creating the uneven rows.

critique.good: Narrower than r2A at 759px and reduces horizontal overflow to 399px; endpoint and qualifiers remain intact.
critique.problems: Description at 244px is too narrow: long rows become four lines, table height grows to 415px, and the one-line endpoint paths leave large blank areas beneath them. Rows feel tall and empty, breaking row-as-unit scanning. It still overflows by 399px.
critique.cause: Description 244px gives only 223px of text, so the 670px prose wraps to four lines. Endpoint remains 282px, so the extra height appears as dead space under short endpoint cells.

critique.good: All descriptions fit on one line, giving uniform 36px rows and very easy prose reading.
critique.problems: The 691px Description column dominates: total width 1206px, overflow 846px. Method, Auth and Rate limit are pushed far right; the first viewport shows only Endpoint and Method, so the compact constraints are effectively hidden. The reader must scroll a long way to connect a row's description with its endpoint.
critique.cause: Description 691px gives 670px of text, exactly the longest one-line width. With Endpoint 282, Method 76, Auth 67, Rate 89, the total is 1205px, so the one-line goal costs 846px of overflow.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r1B.why: Endpoint paths and methods stay intact, but the very tall rows leave large empty areas in the visible columns and make comparison slower.

r2A.why: Paths and methods remain intact, and the comparatively compact rows make the visible portion easy to scan. The remaining columns require horizontal scrolling.

ref_auto.why: Extremely tall rows separate the endpoints so far that comparison becomes difficult, with substantial empty space in the visible columns.

ref_equal.why: All columns fit in the viewport, but endpoint paths, headers, methods and description words split across lines. The resulting narrow columns make the table very difficult to read.

r3A.why: Intact paths and compact rows give the visible columns a clear rhythm, though the rest of the table requires horizontal scrolling.

r1A.why: Paths and methods remain intact, but the taller rows create more empty space than B or E and the remaining columns require horizontal scrolling.

raw.unsure: The supplied images show only a sliver of the columns beyond Method in A, B, C, E and F. I cannot assess their widths, wrapping or full scrolling distance, so the ranking among those layouts is tentative.

r3A.why: Endpoint paths and methods remain intact, but most columns require horizontal scrolling. The visible rows have a reasonably steady rhythm.

r2A.why: Endpoint paths and methods are easy to scan, and the visible rows are relatively compact. The remaining columns require horizontal scrolling.

r1B.why: The intact paths are readable, but the tall rows leave large gaps between entries and make comparison slower. Most columns require scrolling.

ref_auto.why: Very tall rows create extensive empty space in the visible columns, making it difficult to scan endpoints together. Most columns require scrolling.

r1A.why: The paths and methods stay intact, although the visible rows are taller than in B and most columns require scrolling.

ref_equal.why: All columns fit in the viewport, but paths, method names, headers and description words split across lines. The resulting rows are extremely tall and hard to read.

raw.unsure: The supplied views of A–E show only the endpoint and method columns and a sliver of the next column. The off-screen columns cannot be assessed, so B is a provisional choice based on the visible portion.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
